verses.text: Who is like the wise man? And who knows the interpretation of a thing? A man’s wisdom makes his face shine, and the hardness of his face is changed.
I say, “Keep the king’s command!” because of the oath to God.
Don’t be hasty to go out of his presence. Don’t persist in an evil thing, for he does whatever pleases him,
for the king’s word is supreme. Who can say to him, “What are you doing?”
Whoever keeps the commandment shall not come to harm, and his wise heart will know the time and procedure.
For there is a time and procedure for every purpose, although the misery of man is heavy on him.
For he doesn’t know that which will be; for who can tell him how it will be?

There is no man who has power over the spirit to contain the spirit; neither does he have power over the day of death. There is no discharge in war; neither shall wickedness deliver those who practice it.
All this I have seen, and applied my mind to every work that is done under the sun. There is a time in which one man has power over another to his hurt.
So I saw the wicked buried. Indeed they came also from holiness. They went and were forgotten in the city where they did this. This also is vanity.
Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil.
Though a sinner commits crimes a hundred times, and lives long, yet surely I know that it will be better with those who fear God, who are reverent before him.
But it shall not be well with the wicked, neither shall he lengthen days like a shadow; because he doesn’t fear God.

There is a vanity which is done on the earth, that there are righteous men to whom it happens according to the work of the wicked. Again, there are wicked men to whom it happens according to the work of the righteous. I said that this also is vanity.

Then I commended mirth, because a man has no better thing under the sun, than to eat, and to drink, and to be joyful: for that will accompany him in his labor all the days of his life which God has given him under the sun.
When I applied my heart to know wisdom, and to see the business that is done on the earth (for also there is that neither day nor night sees sleep with his eyes),

then I saw all the work of God, that man can’t find out the work that is done under the sun, because however much a man labors to seek it out, yet he won’t find it. Yes even though a wise man thinks he can comprehend it, he won’t be able to find it.

footnotes.content: I've watched how wisdom settles into a person's whole bearing—not just their words, but the way they meet the world. When someone's lived close to God, that peace shows in their face, calming what might otherwise harden into worry or bitterness. Wisdom isn't hidden; it shines.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Preacher speaks plainly here—keep your word to the king, to the powers set over you. This isn't about flattery; it's about honoring the oath we make, the bonds we keep. Even under earthly rule, there's a deeper loyalty: to God, who sees all oaths.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Don't rush away from authority in anger, and don't cling to wrong—the king's will is final here on earth. But the Preacher knows something deeper: there's a God whose will outlasts all earthly power. Patience isn't weakness; it's the clarity to see which battles truly matter.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Authority doesn't answer to us—the king speaks and none can challenge him. This reality humbles us. But I've learned it also frees us: if earthly power answers to no one here, then we're not bound to its approval. Only God's word can truly bind our conscience.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The wise heart knows the "time and procedure"—not just *what* to do, but *when* and *how*. This is no mere cleverness; it's the wisdom that waits on God, that discerns seasons. My own foolish haste has taught me this: God's timing is gentler than my rushing ever was.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: There's a right time for every purpose under heaven, yet the weight of being human is real and heavy. The Preacher doesn't deny our sorrow; he acknowledges it even as he points to God's ordering. Both are true: there is divine purpose, and we do bear true sorrow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: We cannot know what will be, and none can tell us. This is humbling and, strangely, comforting—I'm not meant to carry the burden of the future. My Father knows what lies ahead. I'm called only to walk today with Him and trust His hand on tomorrow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No one can cage the spirit or order the day of death—we are not in control. Neither, the Preacher notes, does wickedness escape its fate; no one can discharge themselves from war's consequences. There is a reckoning we cannot outrun, a truth that should pierce our pride.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: I've watched power corrupt: one person wielding it against another for harm. The Preacher saw this clearly under the sun. Yet Christ came among us *without* grasping power, serving the very ones who held it against Him. There is another way.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The wicked are buried and forgotten, their place in the city erased as if they never were. We think fame matters, that our name will echo—but the Preacher shows it fades. Only what we do in faith, in the sight of God, truly endures. That is worth our care.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When judgment is slow, hearts harden toward evil. I've seen this in myself and others: delayed consequence feeds presumption. This is why grace moves quickly, why God acted in Christ before we could calcify in our sin. Swift mercy breaks through in a way judgment delayed cannot.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sinner may prosper a hundred times over and live long—and yet. The Preacher holds fast to this: those who fear God, who bow before Him, will have better. Not always visible; often hidden from sight. But it is true because God is true.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The wicked won't lengthen their days like a shadow lengthens—there is a limit, a boundary that fear of God does not cross. Without reverence, we trade real life for a shadow of life, brief and empty. To fear God is to live; to fear Him not is to dwindle.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This is the scandal of the sun: righteous ones suffer as the wicked deserve, and wicked ones prosper as the righteous might. The Preacher calls it vanity, and it *is*—under the sun, where God is not in sight. But under heaven, where He reigns, there is a deeper justice coming.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eat, drink, be joyful—these aren't escapes from meaning but companions to honest labor. The Preacher says it plainly: these simple gifts will walk with you all your working days as God has given them. To receive them with thankfulness is a form of worship, a way of saying yes to the life we've been given.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Preacher gave his heart to wisdom, kept his eyes open to all that happens—work so deep it stole sleep, the sleeplessness of one who truly seeks. Yet even then, with all that effort, completion eluded him. There are mysteries we cannot solve; we can only bow before them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this closing: we labor to understand God's work, to comprehend what He does beneath the sun—and we cannot. Yet we know now what the Preacher could only glimpse: in Christ, the work of God is revealed. We see the one who holds it all together, though we still won't fully grasp the infinite.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
